Chapter overview

Contributions of Thanthai Periyar examines his public life from Erode municipal service and Congress politics to Self-Respect, rationalism, women’s emancipation, Anti-Hindi mobilisation, Dravidar Kazhagam and his continuing institutional legacy.

Early life & CongressSelf-Respect & printCaste, reason & womenJustice Party & DKLater campaigns & legacy
Birth, Family and Early Life

Periyar’s early life in Erode, family background, independent learning and formative encounters with caste shaped his later public criticism of inherited authority.

Birth

Erode Venkatappa Ramasamy was born on:

  • 17 September 1879
  • At Erode
  • In the then Madras Presidency

His parents were:

  • Venkatappa Naicker
  • Chinnathayammal, also referred to in some accounts as Muthammal

He was later popularly known as:

  • E. V. Ramasamy
  • E.V.R.
  • Periyar
  • Thanthai Periyar

“Periyar” broadly means:

  • Great person
  • Respected elder
  • Great leader

The honorific became widely associated with him through the Tamil social-reform movement.

Family Background

Periyar was born into a prosperous trading family.

His family’s economic position gave him early experience in:

  • Business
  • Property management
  • Charity
  • Public dealings
  • Local administration

He did not complete an extended formal school education.

Much of his later knowledge developed through:

  • Independent reading
  • Travel
  • Public debate
  • Political activity
  • Observation of social practices
Early Marriage

He married:

  • Nagammai
  • In 1898

Nagammai later became an important participant in:

  • Temperance campaigns
  • Vaikom-related mobilisation
  • Self-Respect activities
  • Women’s political participation
Formative Experiences

Accounts of Periyar’s early life emphasise his encounters with:

  • Caste discrimination
  • Religious hypocrisy
  • Unequal treatment
  • Social exclusion
  • Ritual authority

A frequently discussed episode concerns his experience at a charitable feeding institution in Kashi or Varanasi, where caste restrictions reportedly affected access to food.

The exact details of such biographical episodes vary across later accounts.

Their broader importance lies in the way Periyar used personal experience to criticise:

  • Caste-based charity
  • Claims of religious equality
  • Ritual purity
  • Hereditary social privilege
Intellectual Formation

Periyar did not emerge from a conventional university or literary career.

His thought developed from:

  • Practical experience
  • Public administration
  • Congress politics
  • Anti-caste agitation
  • International travel
  • Journalism
  • Continuous debate

He became known for converting complex social questions into language understandable to ordinary people. His official biographical record identifies Erode as his birthplace and 17 September 1879 as his date of birth.

Business, Municipal Administration and Public Service

His business and municipal experience gave him practical knowledge of taxation, sanitation, water supply, institutional management and the relationship between administration and social access.

Business Career

Periyar participated in the family’s commercial activities in Erode.

His experience as a trader gave him familiarity with:

  • Markets
  • Taxation
  • Local economic conditions
  • Labour relations
  • Public administration
  • Community networks
Municipal Involvement

Before becoming a full-time movement leader, he held several local public positions.

He became associated with:

  • Erode municipal administration
  • Public-health measures
  • Water supply
  • Sanitation
  • Local taxation
  • Public facilities

He served as:

  • Chairman of the Erode Municipality
Administrative Reputation

His public-service career is associated with attention to:

  • Clean drinking water
  • Improvement of roads
  • Removal of encroachments
  • Sanitation
  • Administrative efficiency
Public Service and Social Reform

Municipal experience helped him understand that social change required:

  • Administrative authority
  • Public finance
  • Institutional enforcement
  • Access to common facilities

Questions such as water access and road use were closely connected with caste because marginalised communities could be excluded from common resources.

Resignation from Positions

When Periyar entered national political activity, he resigned from several honorary and municipal positions.

This reflected his movement from:

  • Local administration
  • To full-time political and social activism
Historical Importance

His municipal career is important because it shows that he was not only:

  • A public speaker
  • A social critic
  • A movement ideologue

He also possessed experience in:

  • Administration
  • Business
  • Local governance
  • Institutional management
Congress Career and the Non-Cooperation Movement

Periyar’s Congress phase combined Non-Cooperation, khadi and mass organisation with a growing insistence that political freedom must include social equality.

Entry into Congress

Periyar joined the Indian National Congress during the period of expanding Gandhian mass politics.

He was attracted by programmes connected with:

  • Non-Cooperation
  • Khadi
  • Temperance
  • Opposition to untouchability
  • Mass mobilisation
Non-Cooperation Movement

The Non-Cooperation Movement began nationally in:

  • 1920

Periyar supported its principal methods, including:

  • Boycott of colonial institutions
  • Promotion of khadi
  • Resignation from public positions
  • Social mobilisation
Sacrifice of Public Office

He resigned from honorary public posts and reduced his involvement in business to participate more fully in political work.

Congress Organisation

Within the Tamil region, Periyar held important Congress responsibilities.

He participated in:

  • Provincial conferences
  • Organisational tours
  • Fundraising
  • Membership mobilisation
  • Constructive programmes
Khadi Promotion

He promoted khadi by:

  • Wearing khadi
  • Encouraging family members to use it
  • Taking cloth directly to the public
  • Associating khadi with economic self-reliance
Social Reform within Nationalism

Periyar increasingly argued that the freedom struggle had to confront:

  • Caste inequality
  • Social representation
  • Untouchability
  • Religious hierarchy

He became dissatisfied when national unity was used to postpone these questions.

Political Freedom and Social Equality

A central difference developed between Periyar and sections of Congress leadership.

Periyar maintained that:

  • Independence without social equality could transfer power to existing elites.
  • Political freedom would remain incomplete if caste hierarchy survived.
  • Representation had to be guaranteed before dominant groups monopolised future institutions.

This disagreement later contributed to his departure from Congress.

Temperance, Khadi and Social Mobilisation

Temperance and khadi campaigns trained Periyar and Nagammai in street-level mobilisation, women’s participation, civil disobedience and personal sacrifice.

Temperance Campaign

Periyar strongly supported prohibition and anti-liquor campaigns during his Congress period.

Liquor was criticised because it contributed to:

  • Household poverty
  • Domestic violence
  • Debt
  • Loss of wages
  • Social exploitation
Destruction of Toddy-Producing Trees

During the temperance campaign, Periyar is associated with cutting down coconut or palm trees on his own property that were used for toddy production.

The act demonstrated his willingness to accept:

  • Personal financial loss
  • In support of a political principle
Picketing of Liquor Shops

Periyar, Nagammai and other activists participated in:

  • Liquor-shop picketing
  • Public demonstrations
  • Mobilisation of women
  • Arrest-based protest
Nagammai’s Role

Nagammai’s participation was significant because women frequently bore the social consequences of:

  • Alcohol addiction
  • Loss of family income
  • Domestic abuse

Her involvement helped bring women directly into public political activity.

Khadi

Periyar supported khadi as a means of:

  • Boycotting imported cloth
  • Supporting local production
  • Promoting economic independence
  • Mobilising ordinary people
Limits of Economic Nationalism

Although he supported khadi during his Congress years, he later argued that economic nationalism alone could not remove:

  • Caste inequality
  • Gender oppression
  • Social monopoly
Mobilisation Method

The temperance and khadi campaigns gave Periyar practical experience in:

  • Street-level propaganda
  • Village mobilisation
  • Women’s participation
  • Civil disobedience
  • Public persuasion

These methods were later adapted to the Self-Respect Movement.

Communal Representation and Conflict within the Congress

Communal representation became Periyar’s major conflict with Congress because he regarded equal opportunity as impossible without safeguards against inherited educational and administrative monopoly.

Meaning of Communal Representation

In the political vocabulary of the Madras Presidency, communal representation referred to the distribution of:

  • Government employment
  • Educational seats
  • Legislative opportunities

among different social and religious communities.

Periyar’s Demand

Periyar repeatedly demanded safeguards for non-Brahmin and marginalised communities within Congress deliberations.

He argued that public institutions were disproportionately controlled by groups that had earlier access to:

  • English education
  • Higher education
  • Professional training
  • Colonial administration
Repeated Resolutions

Periyar and like-minded leaders attempted to secure resolutions supporting communal representation at provincial Congress conferences.

These efforts faced opposition or procedural defeat.

The precise number and sequence of conferences are described differently in movement accounts.

The central historical point is that communal representation became a decisive disagreement between Periyar and Congress leadership.

Understanding Merit

Periyar challenged the idea that public appointments reflected pure individual merit.

He argued that merit was shaped by:

  • Education
  • Wealth
  • Social networks
  • Caste privilege
  • Urban opportunity
Representation as Justice

For Periyar, representation was not:

  • Charity
  • A concession
  • Hostility towards talented individuals

It was a method to prevent historical privilege from becoming permanent institutional monopoly.

Conflict with Congress

Periyar believed that Congress leadership:

  • Spoke of national equality
  • But failed to guarantee social equality
  • Opposed effective communal safeguards
  • Gave insufficient priority to caste reform
Long-Term Contribution

His sustained advocacy helped make:

  • Reservation
  • Proportional representation
  • Inclusive administration
  • Educational access

central themes of Tamil politics.

Vaikom Satyagraha and the Struggle for Public Access

At Vaikom, Periyar joined a collective struggle for access to public roads and connected everyday mobility with dignity, anti-caste politics and inter-regional cooperation.

Background

Vaikom was located in:

  • Travancore
  • Present-day Kerala

Caste restrictions prevented oppressed communities from using roads surrounding the Vaikom temple.

The Vaikom Satyagraha began in:

  • 1924
Periyar’s Participation

Periyar travelled to Vaikom and joined the agitation.

He participated in:

  • Public mobilisation
  • Satyagraha
  • Organisational leadership
  • Defiance of prohibitory orders

He was arrested and imprisoned.

Nagammai and Women Activists

Nagammai and other women also participated in mobilisation connected with Vaikom.

Their presence demonstrated that anti-caste struggle was not restricted to male political leaders.

Vaikom Veerar

Periyar later became widely known in Tamil movement memory as:

  • Vaikom Veerar
  • Hero of Vaikom
Nature of the Demand

The immediate demand concerned:

  • Right of oppressed castes to use public roads

It was not initially identical to a complete demand for entry into the temple’s inner religious spaces.

Contribution

Periyar’s role was important in:

  • Sustaining the agitation
  • Mobilising support from the Tamil region
  • Linking public-road access with human dignity
  • Demonstrating inter-regional anti-caste cooperation
Historical Caution

The Vaikom struggle involved many leaders and organisations, including local Kerala reformers and Congress activists.

It should not be presented as the work of Periyar alone.

His contribution was substantial, but it formed part of a broader collective movement.

Wider Significance

Vaikom strengthened Periyar’s conviction that caste discrimination was maintained through control over:

  • Roads
  • Temples
  • Public space
  • Everyday movement

Later public commemoration has continued to identify his imprisonment and activism as an important part of the Vaikom struggle.

Cheranmahadevi Gurukulam and Departure from Congress

The Gurukulam controversy exposed caste segregation inside nationalist education and contributed directly to Periyar’s 1925 departure from Congress.

Cheranmahadevi Gurukulam

The Gurukulam at Cheranmahadevi was associated with:

  • V. V. S. Aiyar
  • Nationalist education
  • Congress-linked financial support
Caste Discrimination Controversy

Complaints arose that students were treated differently on the basis of caste, particularly in:

  • Dining
  • Social interaction
  • Institutional arrangements

Periyar opposed the use of public or Congress funds for an institution that practised caste separation.

Principle Involved

The dispute demonstrated a contradiction between:

  • Nationalist education
  • Social equality

An institution could oppose British rule while reproducing caste discrimination.

Demand for Equality

Periyar demanded:

  • Common dining
  • Equal treatment
  • Removal of caste segregation
  • Accountability for public funds
Conflict within Congress

The Gurukulam issue deepened his dissatisfaction with Congress leadership.

He believed that many leaders were willing to condemn untouchability in principle but unwilling to confront caste privilege in everyday institutions.

Departure from Congress

Periyar left the Congress in:

  • 1925

His departure resulted from accumulated disagreements concerning:

  • Communal representation
  • Caste discrimination
  • Gurukulam segregation
  • Priority given to social equality
  • Organisational dominance
Historical Importance

Leaving the Congress allowed Periyar to develop an independent social movement not restricted by:

  • Nationalist discipline
  • Electoral calculation
  • Religious accommodation
  • Congress leadership structures

The Self-Respect Movement emerged in the same year.

Founding of the Self-Respect Movement

Periyar founded the Self-Respect Movement in 1925 to challenge caste, patriarchy, priestly authority and mental submission through social practices as well as public argument.

Beginning

Periyar founded the Self-Respect Movement in:

  • 1925

The movement sought to create a society based on:

  • Human dignity
  • Equality
  • Rationalism
  • Caste abolition
  • Women’s freedom
  • Social representation
Why Self-Respect?

Periyar argued that oppressed people could not become free until they rejected the belief that they were naturally inferior.

Self-respect required freedom from:

  • Caste humiliation
  • Priestly mediation
  • Religious fear
  • Gender subordination
  • Hereditary occupation
Organisational Character

The movement was not initially an ordinary electoral party.

It operated through:

  • Conferences
  • Journals
  • Public meetings
  • Reform marriages
  • Propaganda tours
  • Local associations
  • Women’s participation
Self-Respect Conferences

Conferences discussed:

  • Caste abolition
  • Inter-caste marriage
  • Widow remarriage
  • Women’s property rights
  • Birth control
  • Rationalism
  • Representation
  • Economic inequality
Social Reform in Everyday Life

Periyar encouraged followers to:

  • Remove caste suffixes
  • Reject expensive rituals
  • Conduct priestless marriages
  • Support inter-dining
  • Educate women
  • Question scripture
  • Challenge hereditary occupation
Radical Character

The movement differed from limited social reform because it did not merely seek:

  • Compassion towards oppressed communities
  • Minor modification of customs

It questioned the legitimacy of the entire birth-based social order.

Historical Contribution

The movement created a durable ideological vocabulary around:

  • Suya Mariyathai
  • Pagutharivu
  • Samathuvam
  • Social justice
  • Women’s autonomy

Research characterises the movement as an organised challenge to caste, patriarchy and religiously sanctioned hierarchy.

Publications, Journalism and the Creation of a Public Sphere

Through Kudi Arasu, Revolt, Viduthalai and related journals, Periyar created a mass public sphere for anti-caste, rationalist, feminist and linguistic debate.

Journalism as Political Action

Periyar treated newspapers as instruments of:

  • Education
  • Agitation
  • Debate
  • Organisation
  • Ideological training

His publications reached people beyond formal political conferences.

Kudi Arasu

Kudi Arasu began publication at Erode on:

  • 2 May 1925

It became one of the principal publications of the Self-Respect Movement.

The title may be translated broadly as:

  • Republic
  • People’s rule
Content of Kudi Arasu

It carried:

  • Editorials
  • Speeches
  • Reports of conferences
  • Social criticism
  • Women’s writing
  • Discussions of caste
  • Criticism of religion
  • International political ideas
Revolt

Revolt was an English-language journal associated with Periyar’s movement.

It began in:

  • 1928

Its purposes included:

  • Reaching English-educated readers
  • Presenting Self-Respect ideas outside Tamil
  • Discussing international reform currents
Viduthalai

Viduthalai became an important publication associated first with the Justice Party and later with Periyar and Dravidar Kazhagam.

“Viduthalai” means:

  • Liberation
  • Freedom

It became a major vehicle for:

  • Rationalist writing
  • Anti-caste propaganda
  • Political commentary
  • Movement announcements
Other Publications

Publications associated at different times with Periyar’s ideological and organisational work included:

  • Pagutharivu
  • Puratchi
  • Unmai
  • Other short-lived or movement journals

Their exact publication dates and continuity varied because of:

  • Financial difficulty
  • Colonial restrictions
  • Prosecution
  • Organisational change
Publishing Strategy

Periyar used publication not merely to record events but to:

  • Create controversy
  • Challenge respected authorities
  • Introduce new terminology
  • Encourage public argument
  • Train cadres
Simple and Direct Tamil

His prose and speeches often used:

  • Direct language
  • Questions
  • Satire
  • Repetition
  • Everyday examples
  • Deliberately provocative comparisons
Press Restrictions

Periyar and movement publications faced:

  • Prosecution
  • Security deposits
  • Confiscation
  • Censorship
  • Imprisonment
Contribution

Through journalism, Periyar helped create a non-elite public sphere in which ordinary readers could debate:

  • Caste
  • Gender
  • Religion
  • Language
  • Representation

Kudi Arasu and Revolt became important channels for spreading Self-Respect ideology among Tamil and English readers.

Anti-Caste, Anti-Untouchability and Social Equality Campaigns

Periyar distinguished limited untouchability reform from caste annihilation and demanded changes in marriage, names, public access, representation and hereditary status.

Caste as the Central Target

Periyar regarded caste as a system of:

  • Social power
  • Religious authority
  • Economic control
  • Marriage regulation
  • Mental conditioning
Beyond Untouchability Reform

He argued that abolishing untouchability alone would not remove caste.

Removal of Untouchability
  • Ends extreme exclusion
  • Allows public access
  • May leave caste identities intact
Caste Annihilation
  • Rejects superior and inferior birth
  • Challenges endogamy
  • Removes hereditary status
  • Promotes common human dignity
Opposition to Varna

Periyar criticised the varna system because it classified people by birth into unequal social categories.

He rejected claims that hereditary division was:

  • Divine
  • Natural
  • Socially necessary
Inter-Caste Marriage

He promoted inter-caste marriage because caste reproduced itself primarily through:

  • Endogamy
  • Family control
  • Inherited identity
Inter-Dining

Inter-dining challenged notions of:

  • Purity
  • Pollution
  • Social distance
Removal of Caste Suffixes

Periyar encouraged people to remove caste titles from their names.

This was a symbolic rejection of public caste identity.

Public Access

He supported equal access to:

  • Roads
  • Wells
  • Schools
  • Hotels
  • Temples
  • Public institutions
Adi Dravida Rights

Periyar’s anti-caste programme included demands for the dignity and representation of communities subjected to untouchability.

However, relations between broad non-Brahmin politics and independent Dalit movements sometimes involved disagreement.

Temple Entry

Periyar supported access to public religious institutions as a civil-rights issue.

At the same time, he questioned whether temple entry alone could liberate oppressed communities without challenging the religious ideas supporting caste.

Social Equality versus Replacement of Elites

He warned that replacing Brahmin dominance with dominance by powerful non-Brahmin castes would not create equality.

His stated goal was destruction of birth-based hierarchy itself.

Rationalism, Atheism and Criticism of Religious Authority

His rationalism and atheism treated religion, scripture and symbolism as open to criticism when they supported caste, patriarchy, fear or hereditary authority.

Rationalism

Periyar promoted:

  • Pagutharivu
  • Critical reasoning
  • Evidence
  • Independent thought

He argued that people should question every authority, including:

  • Religious texts
  • Priests
  • Political leaders
  • Family customs
  • His own statements
Atheism

Periyar became one of the most prominent advocates of atheism in modern India.

His atheism was connected to the belief that ideas of divine authority were used to justify:

  • Caste
  • Gender inequality
  • Priestly power
  • Fatalism
  • Social obedience
Religion and Caste

He argued that caste could not be abolished while retaining religious texts and institutions that sanctified hereditary hierarchy.

Criticism of Scriptures

Periyar criticised texts and traditions that he believed supported:

  • Varna
  • Women’s subordination
  • Ritual inequality
  • Divine kingship
  • Brahminical authority
Opposition to Idolatry and Ritual

He organised provocative campaigns involving:

  • Criticism of idol worship
  • Symbolic rejection of religious images
  • Public questioning of epics and mythology

These actions were intended to destroy fear and encourage critical enquiry.

Ramayana Criticism

Periyar criticised the Ramayana as a text that, in his interpretation, symbolised:

  • Aryan domination
  • Northern cultural authority
  • Patriarchal values
  • Humiliation of Dravidian figures

His interpretation was ideological and controversial.

It differed from devotional, literary and historical readings of the epic.

Ganesha Idol-Breaking Campaign

Periyar organised a campaign involving the symbolic breaking of Ganesha images in:

  • 1953

The campaign challenged:

  • Fear of divine punishment
  • Idol-based religious authority
  • Restrictions on criticism
Burning of Texts and Symbols

At different times, he supported symbolic burning or rejection of:

  • Caste-supporting texts
  • Constitutional sections he believed failed to abolish caste
  • Maps or symbols connected with political domination
  • Religious representations
Method and Controversy

His methods were deliberately confrontational.

Supporters viewed them as necessary to:

  • Break mental submission
  • Force public debate
  • Challenge protected authority

Critics viewed them as:

  • Offensive
  • Excessively provocative
  • Hostile to religious sentiment
Historical Assessment

Periyar’s rationalism greatly widened public criticism of:

  • Religion
  • Caste
  • Superstition
  • Hereditary authority

At the same time, his rhetoric remains one of the most debated aspects of his legacy.

Women’s Emancipation and Reform of Family Life

Periyar’s women’s-rights programme included education, property, employment, divorce, widow remarriage, birth control and equal sexual morality.

Women as Independent Persons

Periyar rejected the idea that women existed only in relation to:

  • Father
  • Husband
  • Children
  • Family honour

He treated women as individuals entitled to:

  • Education
  • Employment
  • Property
  • Sexual autonomy
  • Partner choice
  • Divorce
  • Political participation
Opposition to Child Marriage

He opposed child marriage because it denied:

  • Consent
  • Education
  • Physical health
  • Personal development
Widow Remarriage

Periyar promoted widow remarriage and condemned customs that imposed:

  • Social isolation
  • Dress restrictions
  • Removal of ornaments
  • Sexual control
  • Permanent mourning
Divorce

He argued that women should have the right to leave marriages involving:

  • Cruelty
  • Abandonment
  • Incompatibility
  • Loss of dignity
Property Rights

Periyar supported equal property and inheritance rights for women.

Economic dependence, in his view, was a major foundation of patriarchal control.

Education and Employment

He advocated:

  • Education for girls
  • Professional opportunity
  • Equal participation in public employment
  • Economic independence
Criticism of Chastity

Periyar criticised the unequal concept of chastity when it imposed strict control upon women while permitting greater freedom to men.

He argued that moral principles must apply equally to both genders.

Birth Control

He supported birth control and women’s ability to decide:

  • Whether to have children
  • When to have children
  • How many children to have

This made reproductive autonomy part of his women’s-rights programme.

Domestic Labour

Periyar questioned social arrangements that made women solely responsible for:

  • Cooking
  • Childcare
  • Household service
  • Family honour
Political Participation

Women were encouraged to:

  • Speak at conferences
  • Write
  • Organise
  • Lead protests
  • Challenge domestic restriction
Radical Nature of His Views

For the early twentieth century, his positions on:

  • Divorce
  • Reproductive choice
  • Property
  • Sexual equality
  • Marriage freedom

were unusually radical.

Modern scholarship identifies women’s freedom from social, economic and intellectual dependence as a central part of Periyar’s thought.

Self-Respect Marriages and Civil Social Reform

Self-Respect marriage converted social criticism into a practical institution based on consent, simplicity and priestless ceremony, later recognised through Section 7-A.

Purpose

Periyar promoted Self-Respect marriages as a practical challenge to:

  • Caste
  • Hereditary priesthood
  • Expensive ceremony
  • Religious authority
  • Female subordination
Essential Basis

A marriage should be based on:

  • Consent
  • Equality
  • Public declaration
  • Mutual respect
Priestless Ceremony

Self-Respect marriages did not require:

  • Brahmin priest
  • Sanskrit mantra
  • Sacred fire
  • Astrological approval
  • Elaborate religious ritual
Simple Forms

A ceremony could include:

  • Mutual declaration
  • Exchange of garlands
  • Exchange of rings
  • Tying of the thali where voluntarily chosen
  • Signing or public registration
Social Reform

The form made it easier to conduct:

  • Inter-caste marriages
  • Widow remarriages
  • Inter-religious marriages
  • Low-cost marriages
  • Marriages opposed by caste families
Marriage and Women’s Equality

Periyar argued that marriage should not create:

  • Male ownership
  • Permanent female obedience
  • Forced domestic service
  • Loss of independent identity
Legal Recognition

Self-Respect marriages were practised for decades before receiving specific statutory recognition in Tamil Nadu.

The Tamil Nadu amendment inserting Section 7-A into the Hindu Marriage Act was enacted in:

  • 1967

This occurred during the government led by:

  • C. N. Annadurai
Periyar’s Contribution

Periyar did not personally enact the later law.

His contribution was to:

  • Develop the social practice
  • Popularise it
  • Defend its validity
  • Create pressure for legal recognition
Historical Importance

Self-Respect marriage represents one of the clearest examples of a movement practice later influencing state law.

Justice Party Leadership and the First Anti-Hindi Agitation

Periyar’s leadership during the first Anti-Hindi agitation and of the Justice Party moved non-Brahmin politics towards rationalism, language rights and radical social reform.

Relationship with the Justice Party

The Justice Party and Self-Respect Movement differed initially in organisational character.

Justice Party
  • Electoral organisation
  • Constitutional politics
  • Provincial government
  • Communal representation
Self-Respect Movement
  • Social-reform movement
  • Public propaganda
  • Marriage reform
  • Rationalism
  • Caste abolition
Growing Convergence

During the 1930s, both currents increasingly cooperated around:

  • Communal representation
  • Opposition to Congress dominance
  • Anti-caste reform
  • Language questions
Election of 1937

The Justice Party suffered a major defeat in the:

  • 1937 Madras Presidency election

The Congress ministry was formed under:

  • C. Rajagopalachari
Compulsory Hindi

The Congress government introduced compulsory Hindi in selected secondary schools.

The policy generated opposition because critics feared:

  • Linguistic domination
  • Educational burden
  • Cultural inequality
  • Expansion of North Indian authority
First Anti-Hindi Agitation

The agitation developed during:

  • 1937–1940

Periyar became one of its principal leaders.

Methods included:

  • Public meetings
  • Demonstrations
  • Picketing
  • Women’s mobilisation
  • Student participation
  • Imprisonment
Imprisonment

Periyar was arrested and imprisoned during the agitation.

Women’s Participation

Women including movement activists participated in:

  • Public protest
  • Picketing
  • Arrest-based campaigns
Tamil Nadu for Tamils

During this period, demands concerning:

  • Tamil linguistic rights
  • Regional political identity
  • Dravidian political autonomy

became increasingly prominent.

Justice Party Leadership

While imprisoned, Periyar was elected president of the Justice Party in:

  • 1938
Contribution

His leadership transformed the party’s emphasis from mainly:

  • Elite constitutional representation

towards:

  • Radical social reform
  • Rationalism
  • Anti-Hindi mobilisation
  • Dravidian identity

The compulsory-Hindi decision in 1938 and the opposition led by Periyar and Justice Party figures became a decisive stage in Tamil linguistic politics.

Formation of Dravidar Kazhagam and Non-Electoral Politics

The 1944 formation of Dravidar Kazhagam institutionalised Periyar’s non-electoral strategy, Black Shirt symbolism and preference for propaganda over office-seeking.

Salem Conference

At the Salem conference held on:

  • 27 August 1944

the Justice Party was transformed into:

  • Dravidar Kazhagam
  • DK
Periyar’s Leadership

Periyar became the principal ideological and organisational leader of DK.

Major Changes

The transformation involved emphasis on:

  • Renunciation of colonial titles
  • Removal of caste suffixes
  • Withdrawal from nominated posts
  • Rejection of electoral competition
  • Social revolution
  • Rationalism
  • Dravidian identity
Why Non-Electoral Politics?

Periyar believed elections encouraged:

  • Personal ambition
  • Compromise
  • Caste vote mobilisation
  • Pursuit of office
  • Ideological dilution

He therefore preferred:

  • Propaganda
  • Social agitation
  • Intellectual transformation
  • Direct reform
Black Shirts

The Black Shirt Volunteer movement developed during the mid-1940s.

The black shirt symbolised:

  • Protest
  • Social humiliation
  • Opposition to caste
  • Determination to transform society
DK Flag

The Dravidar Kazhagam flag consisted broadly of:

  • Black field
  • Red circle

The colours represented:

Black
  • Oppression
  • Degradation
  • Protest
Red
  • Revolution
  • Liberation
  • Social change
Mass Propaganda

DK organised:

  • Conferences
  • Street meetings
  • Black-flag protests
  • Rationalist campaigns
  • Publications
  • Reform marriages
Split Leading to DMK

Differences developed between Periyar and younger leaders including Anna over:

  • Electoral politics
  • Organisational democracy
  • Independence
  • Political strategy
  • Leadership succession

Periyar’s marriage to Maniammai in 1949 intensified the dispute but was not its only cause.

Periyar after the Split

After the formation of DMK in 1949, Periyar continued to lead DK as a:

  • Non-electoral
  • Rationalist
  • Anti-caste
  • Social-reform organisation

The transformation of the Justice Party into DK under Periyar marked the shift from colonial-era electoral politics to an explicitly non-electoral social movement.

Dravida Nadu, Language Rights and Opposition to Centralisation

Periyar connected language with education, employment and political power, distinguishing his separatist Dravida Nadu position from later constitutional state autonomy.

Dravida Nadu

Periyar advocated a separate Dravidian political unit at different stages of his career.

The proposed territory was imagined in different forms as including:

  • Tamil areas
  • Telugu areas
  • Kannada areas
  • Malayalam areas
Reasons for the Demand

The demand arose from opposition to:

  • Hindi domination
  • North Indian political centralisation
  • Brahminical cultural authority
  • Unequal federal relations
  • Fear of majoritarian control
From Madras Presidency to Linguistic States

The reorganisation of states along linguistic lines weakened the practical basis for a united South Indian Dravida Nadu.

Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam speakers developed separate state identities.

Tamil-Centred Demand

Periyar’s later political language sometimes focused more specifically on:

  • Tamil Nadu
  • Tamil political dignity
  • Independence or greater autonomy for Tamil society
Opposition to Hindi

Periyar opposed:

  • Compulsory Hindi in schools
  • Hindi as the sole Union official language
  • Linguistic advantage in public employment
  • Cultural centralisation
English

He often supported continuation of English because it could function as:

  • A link language
  • A language of higher education
  • A counterweight to compulsory Hindi
  • An instrument of international knowledge
Language and Equality

For Periyar, the language issue concerned not only emotional identity but also:

  • Employment
  • Education
  • Administration
  • Political power
Regionalism and Social Reform

He warned that Tamil nationalism without caste abolition could preserve internal oppression.

A Tamil state dominated by caste hierarchy would not fulfil his vision of liberation.

Difference from Later State Autonomy

Periyar’s separatist position should be distinguished from the later DMK emphasis on:

  • State autonomy within India
  • Constitutional federalism
  • Decentralisation
Later Campaigns, Alliances and Social Interventions

His later interventions against hereditary education, caste monopoly and constitutional inadequacy combined issue-based alliances with sustained anti-caste agitation.

Opposition to Hereditary Education

Periyar strongly opposed the modified elementary-education scheme introduced during Rajaji’s chief ministership in the early 1950s.

Critics called it:

  • Kula Kalvi Thittam
  • Hereditary Education Scheme
Main Objection

Periyar argued that linking school education with family occupations could reinforce:

  • Caste-based labour
  • Hereditary occupation
  • Rural inequality
  • Restricted mobility
Support for Kamaraj

Periyar supported K. Kamaraj in several political contexts because he viewed Kamaraj’s administration as favourable to:

  • Educational expansion
  • Non-Brahmin representation
  • Withdrawal of hereditary education
  • Social opportunity

This support did not mean complete ideological agreement with Congress.

Relationship with Ambedkar

Periyar and B. R. Ambedkar shared opposition to:

  • Caste
  • Hindu social hierarchy
  • Untouchability
  • Scriptural authority

They met and maintained intellectual awareness of each other’s work.

Differences with Ambedkar

Their political methods and organisational contexts differed.

Ambedkar
  • Constitutional law
  • Independent Dalit political representation
  • Legislative safeguards
  • Conversion to Buddhism
Periyar
  • Mass social propaganda
  • Dravidian identity
  • Rationalism and atheism
  • Non-electoral agitation after formation of DK

They should be treated as allied anti-caste thinkers, not as ideologically identical.

Constitution-Burning Protest

In 1957, Periyar and DK organised protests involving the burning of constitutional provisions or copies as a symbolic criticism of the Constitution’s failure, in their view, to abolish caste adequately.

Participants faced arrest and imprisonment.

Caste-Based Hotel Boards

Periyar campaigned against public signs and practices that advertised caste identity or Brahmin exclusivity in restaurants and social spaces.

All-Caste Priesthood

He opposed hereditary monopoly over priesthood.

He supported the principle that trained persons from all castes should be eligible to serve as temple priests.

Temple Entry and Temple Criticism

Periyar simultaneously:

  • Supported equal access as a civil right
  • Criticised temple-centred religion as a source of caste authority

These positions are not identical but were connected through opposition to hereditary exclusion.

Electoral Alliances

Although DK remained non-electoral, Periyar occasionally supported particular parties or leaders based on issues such as:

  • Reservation
  • Education
  • Opposition to hereditary occupation
  • Language policy
  • Social justice
Pragmatic Support

His support could shift according to:

  • Policy
  • Political circumstances
  • Perceived social benefit

This led critics to accuse him of inconsistency.

Supporters interpreted it as issue-based political pragmatism.

Nagammai, Maniammai, Final Years and Institutional Legacy

Nagammai and Maniammai were organisers and institutional actors; Periyar’s final years and post-1973 legacy continued through DK, publications, archives and social-justice institutions.

Nagammai

Nagammai was more than Periyar’s spouse.

She contributed through:

  • Temperance campaigns
  • Women’s mobilisation
  • Vaikom-related activism
  • Self-Respect organisation
  • Movement hospitality and administration

She died in:

  • 1933
Women’s Leadership after Nagammai

Women such as:

  • S. R. Kannammal
  • Moovalur Ramamirtham
  • Kunjitham Gurusamy
  • S. Dharmambal
  • Other movement activists

helped build the Self-Respect public sphere.

Maniammai

Maniammai became closely associated with Periyar’s later organisational work.

She contributed through:

  • Movement administration
  • Publication work
  • Institutional management
  • Care during Periyar’s old age
  • Continuation of DK activity
Marriage to Maniammai

Periyar married Maniammai in:

  • 1949

The marriage became controversial because of:

  • Their age difference
  • Questions of organisational succession
  • Property and institutional control
  • Existing tensions within DK
Organisational Split

The marriage intensified the division that led Anna and his supporters to form DMK.

However, the split also arose from earlier differences concerning:

  • Electoral participation
  • Independence
  • Party democracy
  • Generational leadership
  • Political strategy
Final Years

Periyar continued to:

  • Travel
  • Speak
  • Write
  • Organise protests
  • Conduct campaigns

even at an advanced age.

Death

Periyar died on:

  • 24 December 1973

He was aged:

  • 94
Continuation under Maniammai

After his death, Maniammai led Dravidar Kazhagam and continued its:

  • Rationalist work
  • Publications
  • Social campaigns
  • Institutional management
Institutions

Periyar’s name and legacy became associated with:

  • Educational institutions
  • Research centres
  • Memorials
  • Publications
  • Social-justice organisations
  • Rationalist movements
Periyar Thidal

Periyar Thidal in Chennai became an important centre connected with:

  • Dravidar Kazhagam
  • Viduthalai
  • Periyar institutions
  • Archival and ideological activity
Enduring Political Legacy

His influence can be seen in Tamil Nadu’s political commitment to:

  • Reservation
  • Social justice
  • Self-Respect marriages
  • Women’s advancement
  • Tamil language rights
  • Opposition to compulsory Hindi
  • Welfare-oriented government
National and International Significance

Periyar is studied as:

  • An anti-caste thinker
  • A rationalist
  • A critic of patriarchy
  • A regional political ideologue
  • A leader of non-electoral social transformation
Balanced Assessment

Periyar transformed public debate by making caste, religion, gender and language subjects of mass political discussion.

His legacy is also debated because of:

  • Harsh rhetoric
  • Religious iconoclasm
  • Generalisations about communities
  • Separatist demands
  • Political alliances
  • Organisational centralisation

Historical assessment should recognise both:

  • His major contribution to social democratisation
  • The controversies and limitations of his methods

Periyar lived from 17 September 1879 to 24 December 1973 and devoted his mature political life principally to anti-caste, rationalist and Self-Respect mobilisation.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The concluding topic consolidates chronology, titles, organisations, publications, campaigns, achievements, controversies and high-yield distinctions for TNPSC revision.

Essential Chronology
  • 17 September 1879 — Periyar born at Erode
  • 1898 — Married Nagammai
  • Early twentieth century — Business and municipal public service in Erode
  • 1920 — Active participation in Non-Cooperation-era Congress politics
  • 1921–1922 — Temperance and liquor-shop campaigns
  • 1924 — Joined Vaikom Satyagraha
  • 1925 — Left the Indian National Congress
  • 1925 — Founded the Self-Respect Movement
  • 2 May 1925 — Kudi Arasu began publication
  • 1928 — Revolt began publication
  • Late 1920s — Self-Respect marriages and conferences expanded
  • 1933 — Nagammai died
  • 1937–1940 — First Anti-Hindi agitation
  • 1938 — Periyar elected president of the Justice Party
  • 27 August 1944 — Justice Party transformed into Dravidar Kazhagam
  • Mid-1940s — Black Shirt movement developed
  • 1949 — Periyar married Maniammai
  • 1949 — Anna and associates formed DMK following organisational differences
  • 1953 — Ganesha idol-breaking campaign
  • 1953–1954 — Opposition to hereditary education scheme
  • 1957 — Anti-caste constitutional protest and arrests
  • 1967 — Self-Respect marriages gained statutory recognition in Tamil Nadu
  • 24 December 1973 — Periyar died
  • After 1973 — Maniammai continued DK leadership
Title–Association
  • E. V. Ramasamy — Original public name
  • E.V.R. — Common abbreviated form
  • Periyar — Great person or respected elder
  • Thanthai Periyar — Father Periyar
  • Vaikom Veerar — Title associated with Vaikom participation
Organisation–Association
  • Indian National Congress — Early political career
  • Self-Respect Movement — Founder
  • Justice Party — President from 1938
  • Dravidar Kazhagam — Principal founder-leader after 1944
  • DMK — Formed by Anna after separation from Periyar’s DK
Publication–Association
  • Kudi Arasu — Major Self-Respect Tamil weekly
  • Revolt — English journal
  • Viduthalai — Justice Party and later DK daily/publication
  • Pagutharivu — Rationalist publication
  • Unmai — Later rationalist journal
Campaign–Contribution Association
  • Temperance — Liquor-shop picketing and personal sacrifice
  • Vaikom — Public-road rights and anti-untouchability
  • Communal representation — Inclusive government employment
  • Gurukulam controversy — Opposition to caste segregation in education
  • Self-Respect Movement — Human dignity and social revolution
  • Self-Respect marriage — Priestless, consent-based marriage
  • Anti-Hindi agitation — Linguistic equality
  • Kula Kalvi opposition — Rejection of hereditary occupation
  • All-caste priesthood — Opposition to hereditary religious monopoly
  • Dravida Nadu — Resistance to political and cultural centralisation
Periyar’s Major Contributions
  • Made caste abolition a central political issue
  • Popularised rationalism among ordinary people
  • Founded the Self-Respect Movement
  • Developed Self-Respect marriages
  • Expanded women’s-rights discourse
  • Advocated reservation and communal representation
  • Challenged hereditary priesthood
  • Led major Anti-Hindi mobilisation
  • Transformed the Justice Party into DK
  • Created a powerful print and propaganda network
  • Linked language rights with employment and political power
  • Encouraged removal of caste suffixes
  • Opposed hereditary education
  • Promoted inter-caste and widow remarriage
  • Developed a non-electoral model of social agitation
High-Yield Distinctions
Periyar’s Congress Phase versus Self-Respect Phase

Congress phase

  • Non-Cooperation
  • Khadi
  • Temperance
  • National mobilisation
  • Communal-representation demands

Self-Respect phase

  • Independent social movement
  • Caste abolition
  • Rationalism
  • Marriage reform
  • Women’s emancipation
Vaikom Road Rights versus Temple Entry

Vaikom immediate demand

  • Access to roads surrounding the temple

Temple entry

  • Access to the temple itself

The Vaikom Satyagraha should not be described simply as an inner-temple-entry campaign.

Untouchability Removal versus Caste Annihilation

Untouchability removal

  • Ends the most extreme exclusion
  • May retain caste categories

Caste annihilation

  • Rejects the entire birth-based hierarchy
  • Challenges endogamy and hereditary status

Periyar demanded the latter, not only the former.

Communal Representation versus Economic Aid

Communal representation

  • Corrects social monopoly
  • Promotes institutional representation

Economic aid

  • Assists those facing poverty
  • Does not necessarily correct caste under-representation
Self-Respect Movement versus Justice Party

Self-Respect Movement

  • Founded by Periyar in 1925
  • Social-reform movement
  • Rationalism and caste abolition

Justice Party

  • Founded in 1916
  • Electoral political party
  • Communal representation

Periyar founded the Self-Respect Movement, not the original Justice Party.

Justice Party versus Dravidar Kazhagam

Justice Party

  • Electoral
  • Provincial ministries
  • Colonial constitutional politics

Dravidar Kazhagam

  • Formed in 1944
  • Non-electoral
  • Social-revolutionary propaganda
DK versus DMK

DK

  • Periyar
  • Non-electoral
  • Social transformation

DMK

  • Anna
  • Founded in 1949
  • Electoral political party
Rationalism versus Atheism

Rationalism

  • Method based on evidence and enquiry

Atheism

  • Rejection of belief in God

Periyar promoted both, but they are not identical concepts.

Anti-Brahminism versus Hatred by Birth

Anti-Brahminism in Periyar’s discourse

  • Opposition to Brahminical hierarchy
  • Criticism of hereditary monopoly
  • Attack on scriptural caste authority

Hatred based solely on birth

  • Reproduces birth-based judgement
  • Conflicts with universal equality

His rhetoric was often broader and more confrontational than this analytical distinction, which remains a source of debate.

Self-Respect Marriage versus Section 7-A

Self-Respect marriage movement

  • Began in the late 1920s
  • Social-reform practice

Section 7-A

  • Statutory recognition
  • Enacted through Tamil Nadu amendment in 1967

Periyar developed the practice; Anna’s government provided legal recognition.

Dravida Nadu versus State Autonomy

Dravida Nadu

  • Separate political unit
  • Supported by Periyar and early Dravidian organisations

State autonomy

  • Greater powers within India
  • Later principal DMK position
Periyar versus Anna

Periyar

  • Preferred non-electoral social revolution
  • Led DK
  • Used iconoclastic rationalist propaganda

Anna

  • Supported electoral democracy
  • Founded DMK
  • Used literature, theatre and parliamentary politics

Their complete comparison should be made after Chapter 29.

Historical Achievements
  • Created mass awareness of caste as an institutional system
  • Shifted social reform from charity to rights
  • Made women’s autonomy a central political question
  • Contributed to the normalisation of reservation discourse
  • Challenged religious and literary authority
  • Expanded political participation among non-elite communities
  • Influenced Tamil Nadu’s legal and welfare framework
  • Established a continuing rationalist organisational tradition
Debates and Limitations
  • His religious criticism was viewed by many believers as offensive.
  • His rhetoric sometimes generalised entire communities.
  • Non-Brahmin unity did not automatically resolve Dalit oppression.
  • His Dravida Nadu demand gained limited support outside Tamil politics.
  • His rejection of elections limited DK’s direct legislative role.
  • Organisational leadership became highly centralised.
  • His support for different political leaders appeared inconsistent to critics.
  • Social reform did not fully eliminate caste, patriarchy or economic inequality.
Exam Traps
  • Periyar was born on 17 September 1879, not in 1889.
  • His birthplace was Erode.
  • His original name was Erode Venkatappa Ramasamy.
  • Nagammai was an activist, not merely Periyar’s spouse.
  • Periyar participated in the Congress before founding the Self-Respect Movement.
  • He supported Non-Cooperation, khadi and temperance during his Congress phase.
  • The Vaikom Satyagraha began in 1924.
  • Vaikom initially concerned access to public roads around the temple.
  • Periyar was an important participant, but not the sole leader of Vaikom.
  • He left Congress in 1925.
  • Communal representation was a major cause of his conflict with Congress.
  • The Cheranmahadevi Gurukulam dispute concerned caste-based segregation.
  • The Self-Respect Movement began in 1925.
  • Kudi Arasu began on 2 May 1925.
  • Revolt was an English-language journal.
  • Periyar promoted caste annihilation, not merely removal of untouchability.
  • Self-Respect marriages existed long before legal recognition in 1967.
  • Periyar founded the Self-Respect Movement, not the original Justice Party.
  • The Justice Party was founded in 1916 by earlier non-Brahmin leaders.
  • Periyar became Justice Party president in 1938.
  • The first major Anti-Hindi agitation occurred during 1937–1940.
  • Justice Party became Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944.
  • DK rejected electoral competition.
  • The DK flag contains a red circle on a black background.
  • DMK was founded by Anna and associates in 1949.
  • The Periyar–Anna division was not caused only by Periyar’s marriage to Maniammai.
  • Periyar opposed the hereditary education scheme.
  • Periyar and Ambedkar shared anti-caste objectives but used different political methods.
  • Rationalism, atheism and secularism are related but distinct concepts.
  • Dravida Nadu and state autonomy are not identical.
  • Periyar died on 24 December 1973.
  • Maniammai continued DK after Periyar’s death.
  • General Self-Respect principles belong to Chapter 26.
  • General Dravidian principles belong to Chapter 27.
  • Anna’s complete contributions belong to Chapter 29.

pyq.q:
Which of the following statement/s is/are true?
Assertion (A) :
A Tamil weekly called “Dravida Nadu” was started by Periyar
to propagate the idea of a separate state “Dravida Nadu”.
